case_brief.incident_description: Lerato was a regional sales coordinator employed for three years. In August she was told that her sales figures were below target. She says the targets had been increased by 35% while two vacancies in her team remained unfilled. She was never placed on a formal performance improvement plan. She had two coaching meetings over three weeks but no written improvement plan, no agreed milestones and no additional resources. She was dismissed for poor performance after the second coaching meeting.
case_brief.original_client_narrative: My targets went up 35 percent while we were two people short. They called two meetings coaching but I never got a PIP or clear plan. Three weeks later they fired me for poor performance.
case_brief.recommended_next_step: WP letter challenging the adequacy of the performance-management process and the fairness of dismissal.
weaknesses: Employer had raised performance concerns before dismissal

letter:
Background

1. We are instructed by our client, Ms Lerato Ndlovu, in relation to the termination of her employment with Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd on or about 28 October 2026. This letter is written without prejudice and subject to contract. Nothing in this letter constitutes an admission of fact or liability on the part of our client, and all of our client's rights are reserved to refer this matter to the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration or any other appropriate forum without further notice should a satisfactory resolution not be reached.

2. Our client was employed as a Regional Sales Coordinator. According to our client's account, she held this role for approximately three years, although we reserve the right to confirm the precise commencement date and the continuity of her service once the employer's records are available.

3. In August 2026 our client was informed that her sales targets had been increased by approximately 35%. At the same time, and according to our client's account, two vacancies within her team remained unfilled, meaning the increased targets were to be met with a reduced complement of staff. This operational context is material to any assessment of whether the performance standard applied to our client was reasonable in the circumstances.

4. Our client attended two coaching meetings over a period of approximately three weeks. No formal Performance Improvement Plan was put in place, no agreed milestones were recorded and no additional resources or support were provided to assist our client in meeting the revised targets. Our client was dismissed for poor performance shortly after the second of these coaching meetings.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: poor performance under section 188(1) of the LRA: The fairness of this dismissal falls to be assessed first under section 188(1) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995, which requires both a fair reason for dismissal and a fair process. Where the stated reason is poor performance, the applicable guidance is found at paragraphs 19 and 20 of the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, which require that the performance standard be reasonable, that the employee understand what was expected, that the employee be given a fair and reasonable opportunity to improve, and that dismissal only follow once that opportunity has genuinely been exhausted. On the facts available, the targets applied to our client were increased by approximately 35% while, on our client's account, two positions within her team remained vacant. A standard set without regard to the operational resources available to meet it is not easily characterised as reasonable, and the resulting shortfall cannot fairly be attributed to our client's own performance without regard to that operational context.

2. Procedural fairness: absence of a structured improvement process: As set out above, our client attended two coaching meetings over approximately three weeks before her dismissal. Paragraph 20 of the Code contemplates that an employee facing dismissal for poor performance be afforded guidance, instruction, training or counselling, and a reasonable period to improve, ordinarily structured through a documented Performance Improvement Plan with agreed milestones and a follow-up review. No such plan was put in place, and the compressed three-week period, without any written milestones against which progress could be measured, falls short of the structured opportunity paragraph 20 contemplates. Taken together with the operational context addressed above, the performance-management process does not reflect a fair opportunity to improve before the decision to dismiss was taken.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Our client proposes the following terms of settlement, in the interests of resolving this matter efficiently and without the cost and uncertainty of CCMA proceedings:

• Payment of compensation on a total cost to company basis, calibrated with reference to the compensation available for unfair dismissal of up to twelve months' remuneration under section 194(1) of the LRA. This reflects the compounding effect of both the substantive defect in the performance standard applied, set without regard to the team's operational capacity, and the procedural defect in the improvement process afforded, namely the absence of any documented Performance Improvement Plan within a compressed three-week period, each of which independently and together increases our client's prospects of success and the employer's exposure at arbitration.

• Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked

• Payment of any accrued but untaken leave pay owed to our client under section 40 of the BCEA.

• Written confirmation that any pension or provident fund contributions due in respect of our client are paid up to date, and that the accumulated benefit will be dealt with in accordance with the rules of the applicable fund.

• Written confirmation that UIF contributions have been paid up to date, together with a completed UI-19 certificate to enable our client to access unemployment benefits.

• A certificate of service issued in terms of section 42 of the BCEA.

• An agreed reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties, reflecting a neutral or positive account of our client's service.

• An undertaking by the employer and its representatives not to disparage our client to any third party, including prospective employers.

• Confidentiality as between the parties and their respective advisers regarding the terms of settlement, the underlying negotiations and the existence of this dispute.

• To the extent that any record of the performance concerns raised against our client exists, confirmation that our client's personnel file will be dealt with on a clean-record basis and that no adverse finding will be reflected or relied upon.

• The terms of settlement to be recorded in a formal written settlement agreement signed by both parties, with all of our client's rights reserved in full until such agreement is concluded.

The matters set out above expose Brightline Retail SA (Pty) Ltd to a reasonable prospect of an adverse finding at arbitration, together with the attendant cost, management time and reputational exposure of defending such proceedings. Our client holds the relevant records of the coaching meetings and the absence of any documented improvement plan, which will form part of the evidential record should this matter proceed to the CCMA.

We invite a substantive response to this letter within seven calendar days of receipt. Should a satisfactory response not be received within that period, our client's instructions are to proceed to refer this dispute to the CCMA without further notice. All of our client's rights are expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: The Code citation in the first legal claim paragraph is given as 'Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' only once at first mention which is correct, but the paragraph opens its fairness analysis with reference to paragraphs 19-20 of the Code before properly anchoring in section 188(1) as the primary fairness test; it does cite s188(1) first in the same sentence so this technically passes the anchor requirement. However the settlement term proposing compensation does not sufficiently connect the HIGH merit band and specific scoring breakdown (understaffing +2, no PIP +2, no opportunity +3) into a clearly calibrated settlement position beyond generic cap-relative language; for a HIGH merit matter (8/8, merit band HIGH) the compensation clause reads as fairly generic 'calibrated with reference to...up to twelve months' remuneration' without signalling that the strength of the claims (substantive 8, procedural 8) justifies positioning toward the upper end of the cap. This is a mandatory check failure per the HIGH-merit generic compensation rule.
criteria.required_fix: Strengthen the settlement clause to explicitly connect the HIGH merit band (strong substantive and procedural scores) to a settlement position calibrated toward the upper end of the twelve-month cap, for example referencing the combination of both defects as materially increasing exposure and justifying a position at the higher end of the available range, rather than a generic reference to 'up to twelve months'.

criteria.problem: The structure broadly follows the standing order (instruction, purpose, background, chronology, legal analysis, settlement). However the two legal claims largely restate the same operational/procedural facts (understaffing, three-week period, no PIP) in both paragraphs, creating duplication rather than distinct substantive versus procedural development; the second claim heading 'Procedural fairness: absence of a structured improvement process' substantially repeats content already covered in the first claim's substantive analysis, reducing the intended two-part analytical structure to overlapping restatement.
criteria.required_fix: Tighten the two legal-claim paragraphs so the substantive paragraph focuses purely on reasonableness of the standard and the procedural paragraph focuses purely on the adequacy of the improvement process, cross-referencing rather than re-arguing the same facts in full.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Claim 1 references 'a reduced complement of staff' and 'operational context'; Claim 2 again states 'Taken together with the operational context addressed above, the performance-management process does not reflect a fair opportunity to improve' – duplicative framing across both claims.

criteria.problem: The response window of seven calendar days is correctly stated and compliant. The settlement terms are structured clearly in the 3A.10 order (compensation, notice, leave, pension, UIF, certificate of service, reference, non-disparagement, confidentiality, clean record, agreement to follow). However the notice-pay clause wording is ambiguous: it references section 37 (notice period) and section 38 as though offering a choice ('subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, such payment to be made under section 38 of the BCEA') without clearly stating that section 37 creates the entitlement and section 38 is the payment-in-lieu mechanism operating together, risking the appearance that either section independently creates the entitlement.
criteria.required_fix: Revise to make explicit that section 37 establishes the notice period and section 38 is the mechanism by which payment is made in lieu of notice worked, e.g. 'Payment in lieu of notice, calculated by reference to the notice period established under section 37 of the BCEA (or any more favourable contractual notice period), paid in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA.' This removes any suggestion the sections operate as alternatives.

supervisory_assessment.supervisory_summary: The draft is competently structured and faithful to the case brief, correctly sequenced per the 3A.1 body order and the 3A.10 settlement clause order, with no invented facts, no case-law citations and no Schedule 8 reference. However it fails a mandatory current-law check: the notice-pay clause treats BCEA sections 37 and 38 as alternative rather than complementary provisions, which triggers the mandatory redraft requirement. Combined with duplicated reasoning across the two legal-claim paragraphs and a settlement compensation clause that under-calibrates to the HIGH merit band, the Drafting Quality Score is set at 6.5, below the 7.5 floor. The letter should be corrected on these three points and re-reviewed before it is approved for dispatch.
recommended_amendments: Revise the notice-pay settlement clause so that section 37 of the BCEA is stated as creating the notice-period entitlement and section 38 as the mechanism for payment in lieu, removing any 'and/or' or alternative framing.

Differentiate the two legal-claim paragraphs more clearly: confine the first to the reasonableness of the performance standard itself, and confine the second strictly to the adequacy of the improvement process, cross-referencing rather than re-arguing the operational facts.

Strengthen the compensation settlement clause to explicitly state that the combination of the HIGH substantive and procedural scores materially increases exposure and justifies a settlement position toward the upper end of the twelve-month section 194(1) range, rather than a generic cap-relative reference.
Re-run the internal QC checklist after the above corrections and confirm the Drafting Quality Score meets or exceeds 7.5 before finalising for client review.
